intro: Searching for a property trust will near you usually means you want to protect a share of your home for the people who matter to you — often children from a previous relationship — while still letting your partner stay there. It is a specific piece of will planning, and it needs someone who understands how trusts, ownership and family circumstances fit together. iComply can introduce you to a UK wills and probate specialist who will discuss your situation and quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a property trust will usually need
need_lead: The situations below are the ones that most often bring people to this kind of search.
needs: You own your home with a partner and want your share to pass to your children rather than follow your partner's wishes later.
You are worried that if your partner remarries or has a change of circumstances, your children could lose out on the home.
You own the property as joint tenants and have been told that a property trust will needs tenants in common ownership to work.
You want your partner to be able to stay in the home for as long as they need it, with the property then passing to your chosen beneficiaries.
You are making or updating a will and want clear guidance on who should act as trustees and what they should do.
context_heading: Why ownership and trusteeship matter here
context: A property trust will generally only works if you and your partner own the home as tenants in common, so each of you owns a defined share, rather than as joint tenants. If you are joint tenants, the ownership usually needs to be changed first, and that is something to raise with your adviser early on.

The trustees you name will need clear guidance about their role, including how the trust should work and what happens if your partner wants to move or sell. Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated; solicitors regulated by the SRA and chartered legal executives regulated by CILEx are insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Say how you and your partner currently own the home — as joint tenants or as tenants in common.
Explain who you want to benefit from your share of the property and who you want to be able to live there.
Mention whether either of you has children from a previous relationship, as this often shapes the advice.
Say whether you already have a will and whether it has been updated since you bought the property.
Describe who you have in mind as trustees, and whether they know about the role.
Note whether the property is in England, Wales or Scotland, so you are introduced to someone practising in the right jurisdiction.
questions: Do we need to change our ownership from joint tenants to tenants in common before a property trust will can work?
How would the trust affect my partner's ability to stay in the home, and what would happen if they wanted to move?
What powers and duties would the trustees have, and how would they be guided?
Could the arrangement be challenged by family members, and how is that risk managed?
Are you regulated, do you hold professional indemnity insurance, and where will my original will be stored?
What would happen to the trust if my partner remarried or their circumstances changed?

faqs.q: Can I put my share of the home into trust if we own it as joint tenants?
faqs.a: Usually not without changing how you own the property first. A property trust will generally relies on tenants in common ownership, so each of you owns a defined share that can be placed into trust.

faqs.q: Will a property trust will stop my partner from being able to live in the home?
faqs.a: The aim is usually the opposite: to let your partner stay in the home while protecting your share for your chosen beneficiaries. The exact terms depend on how the trust is drafted, so discuss your wishes clearly with your adviser.

faqs.q: Who should I choose as trustees?
faqs.a: Trustees should be people you trust to follow your wishes and who understand the role. It helps to give them clear guidance, and some people choose a professional alongside family members.

faqs.q: Does it matter whether the property is in Scotland?
faqs.a: Yes. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so you should make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction for the property.
